passage:
"Deal time, Francis," said Mum, waving a ten-rupee note. "Ten rupees today, or twenty tomorrow when Papa gets paid."
"Today!" Francis said at once.
His sister Ankita looked up from her book. "Last week Mum asked, ten in a month or twenty in a month and a day. You picked twenty."
"That was easy. Both were far away."
"And tomorrow isn't?"
"The ice-cream cart comes at five. Today is today."
Mum held out the note. "Sure?"
Francis grabbed it. By six he had a sticky mouth and no money. At breakfast Papa said, "Salary's in," and Francis went very quiet, doing the sum in his head.

qa.q: What choice did Mum give Francis?
qa.a: Ten rupees today, or twenty tomorrow when Papa gets paid.

qa.q: Why did Francis think taking ten today was sensible, even though he had picked twenty last week?
qa.a: Francis felt eager and impatient because the ice-cream cart was coming at five, so 'today' felt far louder than twenty tomorrow, even though last week he had waited easily.

qa.q: What could help Francis next time the small reward is only hours away?
qa.a: He could decide ahead, as he did when both were far off, and ask Mum to hold the note until Papa is paid so the cart cannot tempt him.

qa.q: How might Ankita see her brother's choice?
qa.a: Ankita notices he is patient only when both prizes are distant, and she seems a little amused that the ice-cream cart beats his own earlier logic.

grounding: Shows a boy who waits for the bigger amount when both are far off but grabs the smaller one when it is available today.

passage:
My name is Uday and this is about Pallavi didi's scooter. Last month she asked me to wash it every Sunday. She said, "Ten rupees right after, or twenty if you wait till the next Sunday."
When she first asked, Sunday was days away, so I said, "Twenty, obviously. I'm patient."
Then Sunday came. I finished scrubbing, the bubbles were still on my hands, and the ten-rupee note was right there in her hand. Next Sunday suddenly felt like a year.
"Ten, now," I said.
She raised her eyebrows. "So much for my patient boy." I bought tamarind candy and it was gone by lunch. I still think about that twenty.

qa.q: What job did Pallavi didi give Uday?
qa.a: Pallavi didi asked Uday to wash her scooter every Sunday.

qa.q: How did Uday feel about waiting when the note was right there in Pallavi didi's hand?
qa.a: With the bubbles still on his hands and the money in front of him, next Sunday felt like a year, so his earlier plan to be patient suddenly seemed silly.

qa.q: What turning point could Uday use next Sunday to get the twenty?
qa.a: He could ask Pallavi didi to keep the money in her cupboard and not show him the note after washing, so the choice is made before the ten is in sight.

qa.q: What might Pallavi didi think when Uday changes his answer?
qa.a: Her raised eyebrows suggest she is surprised and a bit amused, since only days earlier he had boasted that he was patient.

grounding: Illustrates a child who promised to wait for more money but switched to the smaller amount once it was right in front of him.

passage:
Camp note, Thursday. Amandeep, age 10
On Monday I explained the token shop: two tokens buy a toffee any day, or keep four until Friday and swap them for a kite. Amandeep said at once that he would save for the kite and wrote KITE on his token pouch.
Today, a day before the kite swap, he stood at the counter turning his four tokens over and over. Then he bought two toffees. He told me, "Friday is still far." Friday is tomorrow.
Next step: I have pinned a picture of the kites beside the counter, and he can tick a chart for each hour he keeps his tokens. We'll see tomorrow.
Chandrika, camp coach

qa.q: What did Amandeep write on his token pouch?
qa.a: Amandeep wrote KITE on his token pouch.

qa.q: Why might 'Friday is still far' have felt true to Amandeep on Thursday?
qa.a: Amandeep felt tempted and impatient at the counter, turning his tokens over, because the toffees were right there and even one day felt long.

qa.q: What does Chandrika try so the kite has a better chance next time?
qa.a: The picture of the kites beside the counter makes the later reward easy to see, and ticking the chart gives him something small to enjoy while he waits.

qa.q: How might the other campers who kept their tokens feel on Friday, and how might that affect Amandeep?
qa.a: They will likely be excited flying new kites, and watching them may sting for Amandeep, which could make him keener to save next week.

grounding: Shows a boy who planned patiently on Monday but broke his plan when the small reward was right at hand.

passage:
Saturday
Nani pays me for watering her tulsi and roses every day. On Monday she asked, "Manas, do you want ten rupees next Saturday, or twenty next Sunday?" Easy. Twenty on Sunday! One more day is nothing. I even told Gopika didi I was so patient.
Today is Saturday. Nani held out the ten-rupee note and said, "Or twenty tomorrow, like you said."
The ice-cream cart was ringing outside. I took the ten. I don't know what happened. On Monday it was so easy to wait.
Gopika didi laughed and said, "Mr Patient." Nani just smiled and said I'm still her good boy.
Now I have no ice cream money for tomorrow.
Manas

qa.q: What did Nani pay Manas for?
qa.a: For watering her tulsi and roses every day.

qa.q: How did Manas feel about waiting on Monday compared with Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday Manas felt proud and patient, boasting to Gopika didi, but on Saturday, with the money in Nani's hand and the ice-cream cart ringing, he felt too impatient to wait.

qa.q: What could Manas try next week to stick to his first choice?
qa.a: Manas could ask Nani to keep the ten in an envelope marked "Sunday" and go inside when the cart comes, so the choice is made before the moment arrives.

qa.q: How does Gopika didi see Manas taking the ten rupees?
qa.a: Gopika didi finds it funny, teasing "Mr Patient", because Manas boasted about waiting and then gave in the moment the money was close.

grounding: It shows a boy choosing patience when the wait is far away but taking ten rupees today over twenty tomorrow when the reward is near.

passage:
In the village near Karad, tamarind pods were drying on every roof, and Omkar, ten, had filled a whole sack from the trees behind the school.
Shetty uncle at the kirana shop offered him a deal on Monday. "Ten rupees today, or twenty on market day, Friday."
"Friday," Omkar said at once. "I can wait." His cousin Tushar was impressed.
On Thursday evening, Omkar walked past the shop. A new box of orange ice sticks sat in the freezer. Shetty uncle was closing the shutter halfway.
"Uncle, can I have the ten now?"
"Tomorrow it becomes twenty."
Omkar looked at the ice sticks, then at the shutter coming down. "Ten, please."
Walking home, he licked the ice stick and told Tushar, "Next time I'll definitely wait."

qa.q: How much did Shetty uncle offer on market day?
qa.a: Twenty rupees on market day, Friday.

qa.q: Why did Omkar change his mind on Thursday evening?
qa.a: With the ice sticks right there and the shutter coming down, the ten felt real and urgent, while Friday's twenty suddenly felt too far to wait for.

qa.q: What went wrong for Omkar, and what could help next time?
qa.a: He passed the shop when the reward was close and tempting; next time he could take another road on Thursday or ask Tushar to remind him why he chose Friday.

qa.q: What might Tushar think when Omkar says, "Next time I'll definitely wait"?
qa.a: Tushar, who was impressed on Monday, may doubt it, having just watched Omkar give in the evening before market day.

grounding: It shows a boy who chooses patience when the reward is far off but breaks and takes ten rupees over twenty when the reward is near.

passage:
Class 5 maths teacher's note, Wednesday.
We played a little choice game before the lesson on time. Question one: ten stickers today, or twenty tomorrow? Suraj shot up his hand. "Today!" Most of the class agreed. Question two: ten stickers in thirty days, or twenty in thirty-one? Suraj frowned, then said, "Thirty-one, obviously. It's only one more day." Kunal laughed. "Today it was also only one more day!" Suraj opened his mouth, then shut it. He looked genuinely puzzled. I told the class this is very normal: waiting feels easy when the reward is far off and hard when it's right in front of us. Tomorrow everyone gets the stickers they chose for question one, and we'll talk about how the choice feels a week later.

qa.q: What did Suraj choose in question one?
qa.a: Suraj chose ten stickers today.

qa.q: Why did Suraj look puzzled after Kunal's comment?
qa.a: Suraj felt confused and a little caught out, realising he had happily waited one extra day when it was far away but not when the stickers were close.

qa.q: What could help Suraj be patient when a reward is near?
qa.a: He could picture the twenty stickers clearly, or ask a grown-up to keep the reward out of sight until the waiting day.

qa.q: How does Kunal see Suraj's two answers?
qa.a: Kunal notices they don't match and finds it funny that the same one-day wait felt different to Suraj.

grounding: Shows a child grabbing a smaller reward today but choosing to wait for a bigger one when both are far away.

passage:
Saturday
Dadi said I could have ten rupees today for helping her water the plants, or twenty rupees on Sunday if I helped again. Last week I told Chinmay I'd definitely wait for the big money, because I want the kite at the Sankranti fair. But today the chips man was right outside the gate, ringing his bell. I took the ten. The chips were gone in about one minute.
Now Chinmay has twenty rupees because he waited for his Nana's money, and I have an empty packet. I feel so stupid. Why is it easy to say I'll wait, and so hard when the chips man is right THERE?
Tomorrow I'm going to ask Dadi to keep my money in her tin till the fair. Then I can't see it.
Darshan

qa.q: What did Dadi offer Darshan for watering the plants?
qa.a: Ten rupees today, or twenty rupees on Sunday for helping again.

qa.q: How does Darshan feel after the chips are gone?
qa.a: Darshan feels stupid and regretful, confused that waiting seemed easy last week but impossible with the chips man right outside.

qa.q: Is Darshan's idea of asking Dadi to keep the money in her tin a good one, and why?
qa.a: Yes, because keeping the money out of sight until the fair makes the kite easier to wait for than the chips at the gate.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel with twenty rupees saved?
qa.a: Chinmay probably feels pleased and proud of having waited, and closer to the fair.

grounding: Shows a child meaning to wait for a bigger reward but taking ten rupees today when the temptation is right in front.

passage: At the weekly haat in Sonpur, Tushar and his sister Ganga each had a small basket of guavas from the tree behind their house. "The town buyers come after lunch," Ganga reminded him. "They pay twenty for a basket. Morning traders pay ten." Tushar nodded. "I'll wait, obviously." But at ten o'clock a trader stopped in front of him, flicking a crisp ten-rupee note. Tushar could almost taste the jalebi from the next stall. The afternoon felt a hundred hours away. He handed over the basket. Ganga sat in the shade all morning, fanning herself. At two, the town buyers came, and she walked away with twenty rupees. Tushar looked at his sticky fingers and the empty jalebi paper, and kicked the dust.

qa.q: How much did the town buyers pay for a basket?
qa.a: The town buyers paid twenty for a basket.

qa.q: Why did Tushar sell to the morning trader after saying he would wait?
qa.a: Tushar felt tempted and impatient when the note was right in front of him and the jalebi was so close, so the afternoon felt a hundred hours away.

qa.q: What could Tushar try at the next haat to stick to his plan?
qa.a: He could sit away from the jalebi stall, keep busy helping Ganga, or ask her to hold his basket until the buyers come.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel after the town buyers came?
qa.a: Ganga probably feels satisfied that the long wait in the shade paid off, and maybe a little sorry for her brother.

grounding: Shows a child meaning to wait for a bigger payment but selling for less when the money is right in front of him.

passage: Xin's grandmother in Singapore liked to test him. On Saturday she held out a two-dollar coin. "You can have this today, or four dollars next Saturday." Xin thought about the ice-cream truck that came at four o'clock. He took the coin at once. The next week, she tried again, differently. "Four dollars in one month, or eight dollars in one month and one week?" That was easy. "Eight, of course. The extra week is nothing." But three weeks later, when she offered, "Four dollars today, or eight next week?" Xin's hand went out for the four. His friend Yuki laughed. "You said the extra week was nothing!" Xin frowned. It had felt like nothing when it was far away. Now it felt like forever.

qa.q: What did Xin think about when he took the coin at once?
qa.a: The ice-cream truck that came at four o'clock.

qa.q: Why did Xin choose the smaller amount when the reward was close?
qa.a: When the money was near, waiting felt unbearable and the treat felt urgent, so the bigger amount lost its pull.

qa.q: What could Xin try the next time the wait feels too long?
qa.a: He could picture what he'd do with the bigger amount, or decide in advance and stick to it before the reward is close.

qa.q: How does Yuki see Xin's change of mind?
qa.a: Yuki finds it funny, since Xin called the extra week nothing but then couldn't wait when the day came.

grounding: Shows a child patient when the wait is far away but grabbing the smaller reward when it is near.

passage: At the school fair in Nagpur, the token stall had a deal: ten tokens today, or twenty if you came back tomorrow. Hrithik's friend Nitin said, "Twenty's better, obviously." Hrithik agreed. On Monday, when the teacher had asked, "Ten tokens next month or twenty in five weeks?" he'd chosen twenty without blinking. But now the ring-toss stall was right there, the prizes glittering. "Ten today," Hrithik said. Nitin stared at him. "You'll get double tomorrow!" "Tomorrow's too far," Hrithik said, already running to the ring toss. By evening the tokens were gone and he'd won a plastic whistle. Nitin came back the next day and collected twenty. Hrithik watched him spend them on a remote-control car. He blew his whistle, very quietly.

qa.q: What did Hrithik win at the ring toss?
qa.a: A plastic whistle.

qa.q: Why did Hrithik choose ten tokens today at the fair?
qa.a: With the glittering prizes right there, he felt too excited to wait, so tomorrow seemed too far even though he'd been patient about a far-off choice.

qa.q: What could Hrithik do next time a bigger reward is only a day away?
qa.a: Walk away from the stall for a while or decide with a friend before seeing the prizes, so the pull of now is weaker.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel spending twenty tokens on a car?
qa.a: Nitin probably felt pleased and proud that waiting paid off.

grounding: Shows a child choosing ten tokens now over twenty tomorrow, though he chose patience when the wait was far away.

passage:
Monday. Eshaan's uncle Irfan made him an offer: fifty rupees now, or a hundred rupees on Diwali, two months away. Eshaan picked the hundred straight away. "Diwali is ages away. I can wait."
Saturday, seven weeks later. Irfan chacha asked again, to check. "Fifty rupees today, or the hundred next week on Diwali?" There was a new toy car at the corner shop. Eshaan chewed his lip. "Fifty. Today." Irfan chacha laughed. "You said you could wait!"
Diwali day. Eshaan's toy car had already lost a wheel. When Diwali was far, waiting was easy. When it was one week away, he couldn't. "Next year, keep the money in your cupboard, not mine," he told Irfan chacha. "So I can't see it."

qa.q: What did Eshaan want to buy at the corner shop?
qa.a: A new toy car.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan switch to the fifty rupees one week before Diwali?
qa.a: With the toy car right there and the money within reach, he felt impatient and waiting suddenly felt too hard, though it had felt easy when Diwali was far away.

qa.q: What does Eshaan suggest for next year, and why might it help?
qa.a: Keeping the money in the uncle's cupboard, out of sight, so the temptation of now is weaker.

qa.q: How might Irfan chacha feel watching Eshaan change his mind?
qa.a: Irfan chacha seems amused and fond, laughing gently and letting Eshaan learn from it.

grounding: Shows over two months a child patient about a far-off bigger reward but taking the smaller one when it comes close.

passage:
Pranav, you want your pocket money now instead of double on your birthday? Let me tell you about my twin brother Raju, one Holi, when we were ten.
A month before Holi, our Nana offered us a deal: ten rupees for colours now, or twenty on Holi morning. Raju said, "Twenty, of course. I can wait a month." I took the ten.
But the night before Holi, Nana came round again. "Still want twenty in the morning? Or ten tonight?" Raju grabbed the ten. One night to wait, and he couldn't!
In the morning I had my colours, and Raju had his ten rupees and no shop open.
I, Nikita, still tease him about it.

qa.q: What deal did Nana offer a month before Holi?
qa.a: Ten rupees for colours now, or twenty on Holi morning.

qa.q: Why did Raju grab the ten the night before Holi?
qa.a: Raju felt impatient and tempted, because with the reward so close, ten tonight felt bigger than twenty in the morning.

qa.q: Which moment in the story was the turning point, and what could Raju have done?
qa.a: The night-before offer; Raju could have reminded himself it was only one night, or said no before looking at the money.

qa.q: How might Nana have seen Raju's change of mind?
qa.a: Nana was probably amused, having quietly tested whether a month's patience would survive one last night.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a boy who chose to wait when the reward was far off but grabbed the smaller one when it was near.

passage:
Bhupen had planned it for weeks: on Makar Sankranti morning, the kite seller would bring the big red fighter kite he'd saved thirty rupees for. Waiting a month had felt easy when it was far away.
But the morning came thick with fog, and the seller's cart was late. Every roof already had kites up. Kunal leaned over the wall. "I'll sell you my small green one right now. Fifteen rupees."
"The big red one is coming," Bhupen said. Then a kite snapped overhead and the whole street cheered. His fingers itched.
"Fifteen," Kunal said. "Now."
Bhupen handed over the money. The small green kite went up. Twenty minutes later, the seller's cart came round the corner with the big red kite, and Bhupen had fifteen rupees left.

qa.q: How much had Bhupen saved for the big red kite?
qa.a: Bhupen had saved thirty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen buy Kunal's kite?
qa.a: Bhupen felt impatient and left out with every roof flying kites, so a small kite now felt better than the big one soon.

qa.q: What could Bhupen have done during the wait?
qa.a: Bhupen could have helped a friend fly or held the reel to keep busy until the cart came, instead of spending half the savings.

qa.q: How might Kunal see the deal?
qa.a: Kunal probably felt pleased, getting fifteen rupees for a small kite because Bhupen couldn't wait.

grounding: Shows a child who waited patiently for a bigger reward while it was far off, then broke when it was almost there.

passage:
On Christmas Eve in the Bandra flat, the plum cake sat on the dining table under a net cover. Nani had made a rule in the morning: "A small piece now, or a big slice with ice cream at midnight, after church."
At breakfast Jagdish said, "Midnight. Easy." Midnight was so far away it didn't feel like a choice at all.
By ten at night he was lying on the sofa, staring at the net cover. The smell of the cake filled the room. "Ira," he whispered to his sister, "is a small piece now still allowed?"
"You said midnight."
"That was this morning."
Ira laughed and pulled him up. "Come and help me wrap the gifts. Two hours is a lot of wrapping."

qa.q: What was the reward for waiting until midnight?
qa.a: A big slice of plum cake with ice cream at midnight, after church.

qa.q: Why did waiting feel easy at breakfast but hard at ten at night?
qa.a: At breakfast midnight felt far away, but by ten Jagdish felt impatient and tempted, with the cake's smell filling the room.

qa.q: Why is Ira's idea of wrapping gifts a good one?
qa.a: Keeping busy moves Jagdish away from the cake and makes the last two hours pass faster.

qa.q: How does Ira see Jagdish's request?
qa.a: Ira finds it funny and kindly helps him wait rather than giving in.

grounding: Shows a child who chooses patience when the reward is far off but wavers as it comes near.

passage:
The lane was still pink with Holi colour when Dadi held up two notes. "Remember Monday, Abhinav? I asked: ten rupees on Saturday, or twenty on Sunday. You said twenty, no question."
"That was different," Abhinav said, eyes on the ten-rupee note.
"How is it different?"
"Then both days were far away. Now it's Saturday! And the ice-cream cart is outside right now, Dadi."
Sharmila, his elder sister, laughed from the sofa. "He'll be sulking tomorrow when I show him my twenty."
"I won't!" Abhinav snatched the ten. "Tomorrow is ages."
"It's one day," Sharmila said.
"One day is ages," he called, already out of the door, the cart's bell ringing down the lane.

qa.q: What did Abhinav choose on Monday?
qa.a: Abhinav said twenty, no question.

qa.q: Why does the ten-rupee note feel better to Abhinav now?
qa.a: The note and the ice-cream cart are right here, so he feels excited and impatient, and tomorrow suddenly feels like ages.

qa.q: What could Dadi try next time to help Abhinav wait?
qa.a: She could keep the Sunday reward where he can see it and plan the ice-cream trip together for Sunday, so the later choice feels just as real.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see Abhinav's choice?
qa.a: She finds it funny and expects him to regret it tomorrow when she shows him her twenty.

grounding: Shows a child who chooses the bigger later reward while both days are far off, but grabs ten rupees when it is right in front of him.
